title: Trump Faces Mounting Frustration as Iran Resists Deal and Advisors Clash on Path Forward
excerpt: With Saudi Arabia urging de-escalation and Israel pushing for intensified pressure, President Trump confronts deepening divisions among allies and his own team over the five-month-old Iran conflict.
body:
• Trump has grown increasingly frustrated at Iran's refusal to negotiate, holding angry meetings and making expletive-laced calls to allies as the five-month war stalls.
  • Saudi Arabia's defense minister visited the White House urging de-escalation, while Israeli PM Netanyahu pushed Trump toward intensified military pressure — back-to-back meetings that underscored the crosscurrents facing the president.
  • US officials fear Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps now controls decision-making in Tehran, sidelining the political figures Washington has been engaging, making a deal even more elusive.
  • Only 28% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the war, and Republicans worry the conflict could damage their midterm prospects as oil prices climb above $100 a barrel.

President Donald Trump is confronting a deepening impasse in his five-month war with Iran, growing visibly frustrated at Tehran's refusal to meet his demands as conflicting advice from key allies and his own advisors leaves the White House without a clear exit strategy, according to CNN and Reuters.

Trump convened his Cabinet at Camp David on Friday, hoping to chart a path forward in a conflict that has expanded far beyond its initial scope. But his comments offered few specifics. "I think we just want to win," he told reporters. "They'll get weaker. They'll get a little stronger maybe now. Then they'll get weaker. And then they'll peter out."

Conflicting Messages From Allies

The scale of the dilemma became stark this week when two of Washington's most important Middle Eastern partners delivered opposing assessments in back-to-back White House visits.

On Tuesday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sat in the Oval Office and told Trump that diplomacy with Iran was unlikely to succeed, according to Israeli officials familiar with the meeting. The two leaders discussed options for ramping up pressure, including intensifying military strikes and economic measures.

The next day, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman arrived on an unannounced visit carrying a message from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman: Saudi Arabia wants de-escalation, and prolonging the conflict carries major risks. According to sources familiar with the conversation, the minister's underlying message was that "it's Netanyahu who is pushing for this escalation, whereas the Kingdom wants to de-escalate."

Divisions Within Trump's Team

The external disagreements mirror fractures inside the administration. Trump's top envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner have voiced confidence a deal remains possible. But Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine told Congress last week that Trump's stated objectives cannot be accomplished through air power alone, and raised concerns about dwindling missile defense stocks.

"Air power has its limits."

— Gen. Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

Vice President JD Vance has also expressed reservations about further escalation, according to CNN and The New York Times. Trump himself paused a two-week bombing campaign on July 25 after the Pentagon presented strike plans he decided not to approve — the first time he had done so after signing off on nightly strikes for 13 consecutive days, according to Axios.

Iran's IRGC Tightens Its Grip

On the Iranian side, the prospects for negotiation appear equally dim. US officials and regional partners now believe Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has seized effective control of decision-making, leaving the political figures Washington has been engaging as figureheads, CNN reported.

Internal power struggles within the IRGC itself, where senior commanders are jockeying for control, have made it even harder for the US to identify credible negotiating partners. Trump acknowledged the difficulty in the Oval Office this week, noting that an attempted Iranian strike at US positions had come from "a different group than we're dealing with."

"People want to talk, but they break their words so often. All they do is make me angry. You know, they just make me angry."

— President Donald Trump, speaking at Camp David

Iran's position has remained firm: a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran operates on an "attack for attack" basis and would halt operations only as long as the US maintains its own pause. But the official added that "there is more scepticism than optimism" about Trump's intentions.

Rising Costs and Political Fallout

The conflict's expansion has sent shockwaves through global energy markets. Brent crude has climbed above $100 a barrel after Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen announced a blockade on Saudi oil in the Red Sea, threatening to shut a second major chokepoint for energy shipping alongside the Strait of Hormuz.

For the millions of Indians living and working in Gulf countries, the escalation carries direct consequences — from security concerns to the economic ripple effects of sustained energy disruption on regional economies. India, which imports a significant share of its oil through the Strait of Hormuz, faces mounting fuel costs as the standoff continues.

A CNN poll this week found only 28% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the war. Republican operatives worry the conflict could hurt the party in midterm elections, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune acknowledged the urgency of reopening the Strait. "Obviously, we want success there," Thune said. "The question on the Strait of Hormuz is something that obviously the president and his team are trying to continue to negotiate."

What to Watch

Mediators including Qatar and Pakistan are working to revive diplomatic talks, but a senior US official said resuming direct diplomacy with Iran does not appear imminent. Trump reiterated his threat to strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility, bridges, and power plants if no deal materializes, while insisting in an interview with Fox News that he would prefer to avoid targeting civilian infrastructure. The White House said Iran would "continue to pay" until it comes to the table in what Trump deems "a meaningful way."
image_caption: Camp David, where Trump met with advisors amid growing frustration over stalled Iran nuclear talks.
nri_angle: The prolonged US-Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption are driving up energy prices globally, directly impacting NRIs in Gulf countries and Indian trade routes.
